chapter_theme: Poverty (இன்மை): the world honours a few coins over noble birth, kin and flatterers leave with wealth, and poverty strips away lineage, valour, learning, goodness and even sharpness of mind. For one who cannot help those who ask, the chapter says it is better to leave home and live as a guest or a beggar elsewhere.
structure_note: Observations of how the world treats the poor (281-285, 287) are interrupted by advice to the one who cannot give (286, 288) and close with a picture of fallen fortune (289) and a near repeat of 283 (290). Mudaliar notes the two repeats (288 with 286, 290 with 283) and explains them by the tradition that each quatrain had a different author.

281.reading: Even one who lives with a dyed cloth wrapped round his waist gains standing among many if he has ten or eight coins; those who have nothing, though born into a fitting family, are lower than a corpse.
281.nuance: The ochre or patched cloth (Mudaliar gives both) marks someone of no standing; a handful of coins outweighs it, while noble birth without money counts for less than a dead body. The verse reports how the world judges, without endorsing it.

282.reading: Ghee is said to be finer than water and everyone knows smoke is finer than ghee; but if you consider it, the man in the affliction of want gets in through openings even smoke can hardly pass.
282.nuance: A comic hyperbole of need pressing in anywhere for help. Mudaliar's first reading divides the phrase as இரப்பு இடும்பை, the affliction of begging, and gives நிரப்பு, poverty, as another; Shanmuganar and Pope take poverty.

283.reading: Lord of the forest land where they scare parrots from the millet with stones: when the kanthal does not flower on the high rocky hill, the red-spotted bees do not go there; the poor have no kin.
283.nuance: Kin are bees and wealth the flower: they come for what is given, not for the person. The address to a hill chief borrows the frame of the akam poems.

284.reading: While there is wealth, a thousand gather as servants, like crows at a carcass; when one wanders like a bee, no one in the world asks 'are you well?'
284.nuance: The crows at the carcass make the flatterers feeders on the rich man, not friends. Both commentators make the poor man the one wandering like a bee for food; Pope makes the wealth the thing that flies off like a beetle.

285.reading: Lord of the good land of clustered hills where loud waterfalls wash the rocks: for those whom poverty has seized, the family they were born into, great manliness and their excellent learning all perish.
285.nuance: The three goods named are ones normally thought independent of wealth: birth, character and learning. Mudaliar lists the qualities of ஆண்மை as fullness, forbearance, discernment and firmness, or else as valour.

286.reading: One who lives in his own village but can give nothing to those who come to him driven by hunger had better go away and be a guest somewhere than waste his life staying there.
286.nuance: Who is meant decides the tone. On Mudaliar's reading it is advice to a poor man, matching 288; on Shanmuganar's and Pope's it is scorn for a miser, and Shanmuganar lets 'guest' also mean a guest of the other world, that is, death.

positions.position: The man is poor and unable to help, and is advised to go and live as a guest elsewhere.
The man is a miser who gives nothing, and would do better to leave for another place or the other world.

287.reading: Girl whose teeth outdo the sharp jasmine buds: those overtaken by the affliction called want lose at once not only their good nature but their fully risen sharpness of mind and everything else.
287.nuance: The verse plays on கூர்மை: the sharpness lost by the poor is held up against the sharpness of the girl's teeth. Mudaliar notes that நிரப்பு, literally fullness, is used here for its opposite. Shanmuganar's commentary appears under 286.

288.reading: Rather than live on in one's own village, straitened and blocked and struggling, unable to give to one who asks, it is better to go a long way and live the ruined life of holding out one's hand at row after row of houses.
288.nuance: Begging is ranked above the shame of refusing an asker at home. Mudaliar says it repeats 286 and cites Kural 478 for இட்டு (narrow). Pope's translation is missing for this quatrain.

289.reading: When their means are spent and gone, with the hands that once wore bracelets they pull down branches, pick greens, cook them, and eat the boiled leaves without salt from a folded palm-leaf, living on with broken spirit.
289.nuance: The bracelets on the hands that now strip branches carry the whole fall in one image. Mudaliar cites Kalittokai for குடை as a palm-leaf vessel.

290.reading: Lord of the cool, good hill land whose waterfalls never fail: the bright, humming, spotted bees do not go to the branch that has flowered and finished; those who have lost their prosperity have no kin.
290.nuance: Mudaliar notes it shares the thought of 283. The difference is small: here the branch has flowered and finished, so the stress falls on prosperity once had and lost.

links.note: Both say everyone scorns those who have nothing and honours the rich. 281 adds that noble birth does not help: the penniless are lower than a corpse.

Kural 841 says the world does not count lack of wealth as real lack; 281 says the world counts those who lack it lower than a corpse. Both describe how the world regards the poor. The tension holds on Parimelazhagar's reading of 841's second half as a claim about the world's judgment; Kural 752 sides with 281, so the Kural itself is divided.
Both say the poor lose their own people. Kural 1047 limits it to poverty without virtue, which even a mother treats as a stranger; 283 makes no such exception.
The same bird with opposite morals: the Kural's crows call their kin to share their food, an image of the generous; here crows crowding a carcass are the flatterers round the rich.
Both say poverty destroys the standing of one's ancient family at a stroke. 285 adds valour and learning to what is lost.
Kural 1046 says the words of the poor lose force even when they understand well. 287 goes further: the understanding itself loses its sharpness.

Mudaliar says 288 repeats 286: better to leave the village than live there unable to give. The agreement holds on his reading of 286 as advice to a poor man, not Shanmuganar's reading of it as scorn for a miser.
Both rank begging above a life that does not give: the Kural the hoarder eating alone, 288 the poor man who stays home unable to give.

For the destitute who cannot give, Kural 1050 says the fitting course is to renounce completely, the body included on Parimelazhagar's reading, rather than live off others' salt and gruel. 288 recommends going away and living by begging. Same person, opposite remedies; here the Jain book is the less renunciatory one. The tension depends on Parimelazhagar's reading of 1050.
Both show fallen fortune through food: those who once refused a second helping beg for gruel (1), and hands that wore bracelets cook unsalted greens (289).
The same image and conclusion, bees leaving a flowerless plant and the poor left without kin; Mudaliar notes the repeat.

source_issues: Quatrain 282: the last line reads புகற்கா஢ய with a garbled character, apparently புகற்கரிய.
Quatrain 285: the verse reads க்ழுஉங், apparently garbled; Mudaliar glosses கழூஉம்.
Quatrain 286: Shanmuganar's field also holds the text of 287 and his commentary on it; 287's own Shanmuganar field is not aligned.
Quatrain 288: Pope's translation is not aligned.
Quatrain 290: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.
